text: The bar goes up or it does not, and somebody's day reorganizes itself around the answer. Yoav Shamir filmed at the crossings the Israel Defense Forces man inside the Palestinian Authority, and the subject sets the tempo: long stretches of waiting, then a decision that takes seconds and cannot be appealed. On one side of the barrier stands a job that consists of judging strangers quickly. On the other are people whose ordinary errands run through it. Neither party can leave, which is what makes the encounter filmable and also what makes it grinding. What accumulates across eighty minutes is not argument but repetition, the same brief exchange conducted so often that both parties have stopped hearing it as an exchange. The European Film Award it took for documentary went to a film whose hardest task was outlasting routine.

Hesbjerg Castle has stood in the Danish countryside for fifty years under a man who bought it to make it a monastery and then did not. Jørgen Lauersen Vig is old by the time Pernille Rose Grønkjær starts filming, and the plan is finally moving: a group of Russian Orthodox nuns is on the way, which means the idea he has held alone for half a century is about to acquire co-owners. They have views. A monastery turns out to be less a wish than a specification of roofs, plumbing, heat and the rules of a religious house, and every clause has to be settled with a man whose authority over the building is total and whose version of it has never had to survive contact with anyone else. Eighty-four minutes on what happens when a plan finally meets the people expected to live inside it.

Edwin Honig spent his working life carrying poems out of one language and into another. Alan Berliner, his first cousin once removed, filmed him through Alzheimer's, which puts a relative where the interviewer usually sits and changes both what can be asked and what asking costs. Seventy-eight minutes is a short span for a long illness, and the compression matters: this is not decline reported in stages but a series of visits, each one to a man with less of the shared family past available than the visit before. Berliner is the only person for whom that past is an inheritance rather than a case history, and he keeps coming back with a camera anyway, which is either devotion or appetite and is probably both. The pressure the arrangement creates is not about what a man loses but about who is entitled to keep asking him for it.

Anna Belova has buried two husbands and works the land with her brother Mikhail, who talks. Viktor Kossakovsky filmed the pair in 1992, sixty minutes inside a household whose division of labor is complete: she does the work and keeps the account of it, he thinks out loud, drinks, and pushes an idea until it collapses under its own weight. Documentaries about families usually need an event. This one has an arrangement instead, a brother and sister who have been irritating each other for decades and have no intention of pausing for a camera. The interest lies in how much of two lives is audible in a quarrel about nothing, and in what proximity does to both parties: Kossakovsky is close enough that they perform for him, and stays long enough that performing cannot be sustained.

Fifty-two minutes, which is too long for a short and too brief for the shape a feature is expected to hold, and that odd length is the first decision the film makes. A young woman's mother has died and she sets about assembling a life without her; the register is black comedy, so the film declines the tone that grief is supposed to arrive in. Played deadpan, a death does something particular to the ordinary business around it. The errands stay errands. The small talk stays small talk. Meanwhile the person in the middle quietly revises what counts as normal and does not announce the revision to anybody. Stuart McDonald made it in Australia in 2007, and its method is to treat an enormous loss as a logistical problem, which is nearer to how the first months actually pass.

Everything that reaches Young-Chan arrives through his hands, conversation included. He is deaf and blind; Soon-Ho, who has learned to make herself understood to him by touch, has a spine condition that limits what she can carry and how long she can stand. Their situation is practical before it is anything else, two people whose independence runs through each other's bodies, and Yi Seung-jun films at the speed that arrangement demands, since a sentence has to be delivered by hand before it can be answered. Young-Chan wants to write a book. Soon-Ho cannot always be there, and both of them know it. Eighty-eight minutes at the pace of spelling turns an ordinary household into a set of engineering problems, each solved twice, once with the body and once in words.

The interview happens after the arrest and before anything has been decided, in an office where a deputy prosecutor has minutes to work out what kind of person is sitting there. Raymond Depardon collected fourteen of these encounters and set them one after another: a series rather than a case followed to its verdict, 109 minutes of the same room and a changing cast. Repetition does the arguing. Fourteen times a person tries to account for himself in the only language he has, and fourteen times it proves to be the wrong language for a room where the vocabulary is administrative and the clock is running. The state on view is not angry. It is busy, and busy is worse, because nobody behind the desk intends any harm and the man in front of it is sorted regardless.

Rumidjah has opinions about what her granddaughter is becoming and no leverage over any of it. She is old, Christian, poor and living in a Jakarta slum; Tari belongs to whatever Indonesia is turning into, and between them stand Rumidjah's sons Bakti and Dwi, who are the ones actually handling money. Leonard Retel Helmrich stayed with this household long enough that its economics show up as behavior rather than as a topic: who pays for what, who is owed, who is expected home, which requests can no longer be refused. Filming a family from inside its own rooms keeps the disagreements disagreements instead of turning them into illustrations. Across 109 minutes the largest changes in the country arrive the way they usually do, as small revisions to what a grandmother can ask of the people she raised.

The killing happens early, and the rest is traffic: brothers, bosses and the people who owe them, all moving to contain a single act. Takashi Miike gives it seventy-nine minutes and assumes an audience that already knows how these obligations work, so nobody is explained and nothing is argued for. A hit man is hidden by a nurse. His brothers go looking for him before the dead man's people do. What holds the picture together is the collision of two kinds of family, the one a man is born into and the one he swore himself to, with each turn of the plot forcing someone to choose between them against a deadline. The brutality lands on whoever is nearest. Stripped of connective tissue this way, the film is either badly thinned or exactly as blunt as the trade it describes.

Tayi married a photograph of Hossein, who was in Switzerland studying radiology and could not get home for his own wedding. Their daughter, Firouzeh Khosrovani, tells the marriage that followed through the house it happened in: its rooms, its portraits, the arrangement of a domestic space shared by a devout woman and a secular man. Eighty-two minutes, and the method is reconstruction rather than record, a daughter narrating a disagreement that predates her and was never settled for her benefit. She is not a neutral party and makes no claim to be one. What she gets out of that opening fact is not a figure of speech but a working description of the distance two people held on to in Teheran while sharing one address.

A thousand hours of recorded BaAka music exist because an American heard one song on the radio and went to find where it came from. Louis Sarno walked into the Central African rainforest twenty-five years ago and stayed, becoming part of the community he was recording and raising his son Samedi there. Michael Obert builds the film around an old promise: Sarno takes the boy to America. The trip measures both directions at once, what a child makes of the country his father left, and what the father has turned into, which is a man who no longer fits the world he came from and is depended on by the one he chose. Ninety-eight minutes, two continents, one household's obligations. The archive is the complication, since recording on that scale means somebody already suspected it might not last.

Oleg is twenty-two, and his mother has decided that what is wrong with him can be fixed. Marina calls him autistic and a loafer, a young man enrolled at the University of Nizhny Novgorod who watches television instead of the lectures, and her remedy is a sequence of specialists, some practicing methods that are hard to file under medicine. Jerzy Sladkowski's camera is admitted to all of it, the sessions included, and that access is the uneasy center of the thing: the consent opening these doors comes from the person who is not the patient. Ninety-two minutes with a household where affection and humiliation are administered by the same hand, on a schedule. What hangs over every appointment is which of the two people in the room is actually being treated.
